summary:
Pahang stands under the national framework of Malaysia, and the national assessment governs a visit to the state. Only what is specific to Pahang is recorded here.

The Human Dignity Trust's Malaysia country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, identifies no arrest, raid or prosecution in Pahang. The enforcement actions it documents since the 2018 election took place in other states.

Pahang's own Sharia enactment allows a court to order a person convicted of cross-dressing or a related offence into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months (section 66). Like every state Sharia enactment in Malaysia it applies only to Muslims, and the state provisions carry no legal definition of transgender dressing.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021. Pahang was among the states where interviewees lived, but the release records no Pahang-specific enforcement case, and no dated incident occurring in Pahang appears in the sources reviewed.
tangentialFactors:
For comparison, the enforcement the Human Dignity Trust documents since the 2018 election sits outside Pahang: an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur that arrested at least 20 LGBT people, an August raid on an LGBT venue that arrested twenty men, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and November 2023 plans in Johor for conversion-therapy centres.

The Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report describes national patterns of conversion practices, discrimination and violence against LGBT people, including government-run rehabilitation programmes that at least 1,733 people had attended as of June 2021. Pahang enters that report only as a place where some interviewees lived, not as a site of documented enforcement.
localsOnly:
Section 66 of the Pahang Sharia enactment exposes Muslim residents to court-ordered counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months on a cross-dressing or related charge. The sources reviewed do not name the Pahang enforcement body and record no charge brought under the section.

No Pahang-specific provision on identity documents, health care, employment, public facilities or partnership recognition is sourced. On those matters residents stand under the national framework recorded in the country profile.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether section 66 has been used, when, and against whom is unresolved: no Pahang case, charge or sentence under it appears in the sources reviewed.

No Pahang-specific figure for violence, arrests or discrimination is available, and the sources give no denominator or measurement period for the state.

The Human Rights Watch release does not break out what the interviewees living in Pahang reported, so their accounts cannot be attributed to the state.

The Human Dignity Trust list gives the month but not the year for the August raid on an LGBT venue; the year is unresolved in the source.

No Pahang-specific rule on entry, visa status, document markers or airport screening is sourced.
